1.summary: Habakkuk complains that God ignores violence and injustice in Judah; God answers that he is raising up the Babylonians to judge them, which leads Habakkuk to a harder question about why God would use a nation more wicked still.
1.lookfor: Notice the two complaints and the answer between them, and the image of the fisherman who worships his net.

names.name: Habakkuk
names.gloss: The prophet; the name may come from a Hebrew word for embrace or from an Akkadian plant name.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The Babylonians, whose dynasty took over the empire after Assyria fell.

insights.title: A prophet who argues
insights.body: Most prophets speak God's word to the people. Habakkuk speaks to God for himself, asking How long? and Why? (1:2-3). His questions belong with the laments of the Psalms, Job and Jeremiah, which also bring honest complaints before God.

insights.title: Violence
insights.body: Habakkuk cries Violence! (1:2), Hebrew hamas, the same word used for the corruption that led to the flood. It recurs throughout the book: Judah's violence (1:3), Babylon's violence (1:9), and the violence done to the land (2:8, 2:17). The book is a meditation on what God does about violence.

insights.title: The law paralysed
insights.body: The law is paralyzed, and justice never prevails (1:4). The word for paralysed means to grow numb or slack. Courts and the Torah itself have lost their force because the wicked surround the righteous. Habakkuk may be describing the reign of Jehoiakim.

insights.title: A work you won't believe
insights.body: God says he is doing a work in your days that you will not believe (1:5). Paul quotes this in a synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, warning listeners not to reject the work of God in Jesus. Paul follows the Greek version, which reads you scoffers.

insights.title: The Babylonian war machine
insights.body: The Chaldeans are fast, fierce and self-confident (1:6-11). Under Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar, Babylon destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC and defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC. Building earthen ramps to take walled cities (1:10) was standard siege practice.

insights.title: Purer eyes
insights.body: Habakkuk's second complaint turns on God's holiness: You who have purer eyes than to see evil ... why do you tolerate those who deal treacherously? (1:13). If God punishes Judah, why use a nation worse than Judah? The question sharpens rather than resolves the problem.

insights.title: Worshipping the net
insights.body: The conqueror sacrifices to his net (1:16), meaning he worships his own military power. Assyrian and Babylonian art pictures gods and kings capturing enemies in a net. The Qumran commentary on Habakkuk applied this verse to the Romans, who were said to sacrifice to their military standards.

insights.title: Whose strength is his god
insights.body: God describes the Babylonian as guilty, whose strength is his god (1:11). Power becomes its own object of worship. In what ways might nations or people today make strength their god?

2.summary: Habakkuk waits on the watchtower; God tells him to write the vision plainly and wait for it, declares that the righteous will live by faith, and pronounces five woes on the proud oppressor.
2.lookfor: Notice what Habakkuk is told to do with the vision, the contrast in 2:4, and the five woes, each with its own crime.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead, pictured as never satisfied.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: Mountains to the north whose forests empires cut down.

insights.title: On the watchtower
insights.body: Habakkuk stations himself like a sentry on the walls to see what God will say (2:1). He has asked his questions; now he waits for the answer. Prophets are often pictured as watchmen.

insights.title: Plain on tablets
insights.body: Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it (2:2). This probably means that a messenger or herald can read it easily as he runs, or that it can be read at a glance. The vision is meant to be public and lasting.

insights.title: Though it takes time
insights.body: The vision is for the appointed time; though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come (2:3). Babylon would fall in 539 BC, about seventy years later. Hebrews quotes this verse from the Greek version, which reads it of a coming person, he who comes will come.

insights.title: The righteous will live by faith
insights.body: But the righteous will live by his faith (2:4). The Hebrew emunah means faithfulness, steady trust that holds on. Paul quotes it in Romans and Galatians as "The righteous will live by faith," and Martin Luther's reading of it helped spark the Reformation. Jewish interpreters have stressed faithful living; Paul stresses trust in God rather than works of the law.

insights.title: Five woes
insights.body: The nations take up a taunt against the oppressor in five woes (2:6-20): against plunder, unjust gain, cities built with blood, getting neighbours drunk to shame them, and idols. Each crime brings its own punishment. Plunderers will be plundered (2:8).

insights.title: The stones cry out
insights.body: The stone will cry out of the wall (2:11): even the buildings of the oppressor testify against him. When the Pharisees tell Jesus to silence his disciples, he says that if they were silent, the stones would cry out. The image of creation as a witness runs through the Bible.

insights.title: Filled with the knowledge of his glory
insights.body: In the middle of the woes stands a promise: the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh's glory, as the waters cover the sea (2:14). Isaiah has almost the same line. Empires labour for fire, but God's glory will fill the world.

insights.title: Let all the earth be silent
insights.body: After mocking idols that cannot speak (2:18-19), the chapter ends: Yahweh is in his holy temple. Let all the earth be silent before him! (2:20). The verse is used to begin worship in many churches. Why might silence be the right response to the problems Habakkuk raised?

3.summary: Habakkuk prays a psalm recalling God's coming in power as at the exodus and Sinai, trembles at what lies ahead, and resolves to rejoice in God even if every crop and flock fails.
3.lookfor: Notice the musical notes, the images of God marching from the south, and the list of losses in 3:17 followed by yet.

names.name: Teman
names.gloss: A region of Edom, to the south-east of Judah.

names.name: Paran
names.gloss: Mountain or wilderness in the Sinai region.

names.name: Cushan
names.gloss: A desert people, mentioned alongside Midian.

names.name: Midian
names.gloss: A desert region east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

insights.title: A psalm with music notes
insights.body: The chapter has a title (3:1), the word Selah three times, and a closing note to the music director (3:19), like many Psalms. The Hebrew title, shigionoth, is uncertain and may describe a type of lament or musical setting. The prayer was evidently used in worship.

insights.title: In wrath remember mercy
insights.body: Habakkuk asks God to renew his work in the middle of the years, and in wrath, remember mercy (3:2). He accepts that judgment is coming but asks for mercy within it. The prayer moves from argument to request.

insights.title: God came from Teman
insights.body: God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran (3:3). Old Israelite poems picture Yahweh marching from the southern deserts, the region of Sinai and Edom. The images of earthquake, storm and plague recall the exodus and Sinai.

insights.title: Warrior against sea and river
insights.body: Was Yahweh's anger against the rivers and the sea? (3:8). The poem uses images of God as a divine warrior with horses, chariots, bow and arrows, battling the waters. Canaanite myths told of the god Baal fighting Sea and River; Israel's poets borrowed such imagery for Yahweh's victory at the Red Sea.

insights.title: Sun and moon stood still
insights.body: The sun and moon stood still in the sky (3:11) recalls Joshua's battle at Gibeon. Habakkuk weaves Israel's past victories into one great picture of God fighting for his people. Your anointed (3:13) may be the king or the people.

insights.title: I trembled
insights.body: Habakkuk's body trembles, his lips quiver, and rottenness enters his bones (3:16), yet he resolves to wait quietly for the day of trouble. Faith here does not remove fear but holds on through it. Is it possible to trust God and be afraid at the same time?

insights.title: Though the fig tree
insights.body: Though the fig tree doesn't flourish ... yet I will rejoice in Yahweh (3:17-18). Habakkuk lists the total failure of a farming economy: figs, grapes, olives, grain, flocks and herds. The book that began with Why? ends with joy in God himself, not in his gifts. This is what living by faith (2:4) looks like.

insights.title: Feet like a deer
insights.body: He makes my feet like deer's feet, and enables me to go in high places (3:19) borrows from Psalm 18. The deer moves sure-footed on steep and dangerous ground. God gives strength not to avoid hard places but to walk on them.

intro.who: Habakkuk, a prophet of Judah about whom nothing certain is known; the psalm in chapter 3, with its musical notes, has led some to think he served among the temple musicians. A later legend in the Greek additions to Daniel has him carrying food to Daniel in the lions' den.
intro.when: The rise of the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, is described as happening now, so most date the book to the late 7th century BC, around 610 to 600 BC, in the reign of Jehoiakim.
intro.why: Instead of speaking for God to the people, Habakkuk questions God about injustice in Judah and the cruelty of Babylon, and learns to wait in faith and rejoice in God even when everything fails.
